October 2036. Leo has been a tram driver for two weeks (still with an instructor). Elena rides the M1 to practise listening: announcements, conversations, noise. Leo talks to her at the end of the line.
Well? What did you hear today?

Everything and nothing. I understand the announcements. “Next stop: Eberswalder Straße. Exit on the left.” But the people! Two women behind me spoke so fast that I only understood “rent” and “outrageous”.
Well, that's enough. Then you know what it was about: the rent is too high and they're annoyed about it.
Elif says the same. In the exam I don't have to understand every word, just the main idea. And in some parts you hear the text only once!
Like an announcement. Nobody repeats that either.
And the hardest thing: the task says “The speaker is satisfied with the result”, and in the text she says: “I'd never have expected that, it's great.” Not one word the same!
It's like driving. The signal doesn't say “Watch out, child”. The signal is a red ball in the street. You have to understand what it means.
Everyone says that now. I don't know if it's a compliment.
It is. And now drive. I want to listen to the route back as well. With notes.

If reading had been a matter of patience for Elena, listening was a matter of fear. When reading you could go back, read a sentence again, put a dot in the margin. When listening you couldn't. The words came and then vanished, like a tram you'd missed, and the next one came only ten minutes later, or never. In the first practice listening test, which Elif did with her on the Monday after the reading test, with the laptop and the speakers from the café, Elena didn't understand the first question of the interview in part two, got stuck on it, was still thinking about the first question when the speaker was already on the third, and so lost all five. Afterwards she sat in silence and said something in Romanian that Elif didn't understand and which, as Lena translated later, was better left untranslated.

In the evening she rang Mara, at the hospital, during her break. Mara had also taken her German exams years ago and remembered, laughing, every detail of the listening paper. “At the first announcement I panicked so much”, she said, “that I didn't even hear it. I only heard my heart.” Elena asked her what had helped. Mara thought about it. “Work”, she said at last. “On the ward. Patients don't talk like in the textbook. They talk quietly, in pain, in dialect, without teeth. And still you have to understand whether someone wants water or is dying. That's where you learn to hear the important thing. Not the grammar.” She laughed again. “Mum, you don't need to study any more. You just need to listen to Berlin. Berlin talks enough.”

Elif didn't have a ready-made method for listening the way she had had for reading. She was a child who had grown up with German, Turkish at home, German outside, and had never had to learn how to listen. She simply knew. So she asked others. She asked Grete, who had listened all her life. She asked Leo, who made announcements every day and had to understand the radio messages from control, often with crackling and background noise. And she asked Dr Vogt, who, she knew, had to hear instructions through masks at night in the operating theatre, amid the beeping of the machines. Each of them gave her different advice. And in the end, as Elif wrote in her notebook, it was actually the same advice, just in three different languages: the language of music, the language of the tram and the language of medicine.

Grete said, in a very quiet voice, one Wednesday afternoon at the care home: “When an orchestra plays, you don't hear every violin. You hear the melody. The violins are only there so that the melody can be born. Look for the melody, not the violins.” Leo said, in the depot canteen, between two shifts: “When control radios through, it often crackles so much that you only understand half. But you know beforehand what might come. Breakdown, diversion, delay. You're waiting for one of three words. Then you hear it, even through the crackling.” And Dr Vogt said, at nine in the morning, over the mint tea in the café, after a night shift: “In the operating theatre there's a rule. If you didn't understand something, don't ask about the word. Ask about the intention. What does the surgeon want? Then you know what he said.”

Out of these three pieces of advice Elif made a method, which she wrote on an index card and gave to Elena, to put in front of her at every test. One: read beforehand what might come, like Leo. Two: look for the melody, not every word, like Grete. Three: ask about the intention, not the word, like Dr Vogt. And underneath, in smaller writing, a fourth point, which she had added herself: “If you've missed something: let it go. The next tram is coming.” Elena taped the card into her twelfth notebook, on the first page, above the twenty-three Berlin words.

Then began what Elif called “training in the wild”. Elena wasn't only to listen to exam texts, but to the city. Every morning she rode the M1 for an hour, in Leo's tram when he was on duty, otherwise in another one, and listened. The announcements. The passengers' conversations. The phone calls people made loudly, without embarrassment, so that, as Elena remarked, you learn more about Berliners' private lives in a week than in five years of textbooks. She took notes. Not sentences, just keywords: “Woman with dog, row with landlord, service charges, wants to move.” “Two students, exam, failed, unfair professor.” “Old man, phone, grandson, forgotten birthday, remorse.” In the evening she read the notes to Elif, and Elif said: “That's exactly part one. Short texts, the main information, done.”

Once, on a rainy Wednesday, an elderly woman with a shopping bag full of apples sat down next to Elena in Leo's tram and started a conversation without asking whether Elena wanted one. She spoke Saxon, broad and soft, with vowels Elena had never heard, and at first Elena understood almost nothing. But she remembered the card. Not the words. The intention. And after a while she understood: the woman had come from Leipzig to Berlin sixty years ago, her husband had died last year, and every Wednesday she rode the M1 to the cemetery, with apples, because he had loved apples. Elena answered in German, with her Transylvanian accent, and the woman laughed and said: “Ah, you're not from round here either!” And then they talked, two accents that had met, all the way to the terminus, and neither understood everything, and both understood enough.

The hardest was part three, the discussion, where several people talked over each other and you had to work out who held which opinion. For this Elif had a special exercise. One Thursday afternoon she sat Elena in the café at the table next to Hotte and Ludwig, who were arguing, as every Thursday, about some topic or other, this time whether the new M15 line was a good idea. Elena only had to listen and at the end say who was for and who was against, and why. It was, as Elena said later, the hardest listening exam of her life. Hotte spoke Berlin dialect, fast, loud, with words that weren't in any dictionary. Ludwig spoke standard German, slowly, but with so many subordinate clauses that you got lost in them. And both kept interrupting each other.

After twenty minutes Elif asked: “Well?” Elena looked at her notes. Then she said, quietly: “Mr Kaminski is against the new line. He says it has to go along his old street, where cows used to stand, and that this is against tradition. But actually, I think, he isn't against the line. He's against something he knows changing.” She paused. “Mr Brandt is for it. He says a new line means more people will take the tram. But he says it as if he weren't quite sure. He says «basically» three times. Anyone who says «basically» three times has doubts.” Elif stared at her. Hotte and Ludwig, who had stopped arguing during the last sentences, stared at her too. Then Hotte said: “The lady's right. No idea what I'm against. I'm just against.”

Ludwig said nothing. He gave Elena a long look, with an expression Lena later described as “caught red-handed”. Then he admitted that he did have doubts, not about the line, but about whether he would ever use it himself, at eighty-eight, with his legs getting weaker every month. He had said “basically” because he hadn't wanted to say “maybe not any more”. Elena had heard it. Not in the words, but behind them, in the melody, as Grete had said. She put her hand on his. “You'll ride on it”, she said. “Leo will drive it. And you'll sit at the front.” Ludwig smiled. “That”, he said, “is part four. A lecture. And I'm happy to listen to that one twice.”

The last practice listening test took place on the Monday before the exam, in the cellar, with Elif's stopwatch and Lena's best speakers. Elena sat in front of the laptop, with the card with the four points in front of her, and listened. In part one she read the tasks beforehand, underlined the keywords, waited for the three words that might come. In part two she missed a question, let it go and was right back there for the next one. In part three, the discussion, she thought of Hotte and Ludwig and didn't listen to the words but to what was behind the words. And in part four, the lecture on urban bees, which was heard twice, she had to smile, because she already knew half of it from Dan. At the end she had twenty-two out of twenty-five points. Elif wrote underneath in red: “Melody found.”

Leo, to whom Elif sent the result by message that same evening, replied with a single photo: the screen in his cab, showing the announcement for the next stop, and below it, written in chalk on a piece of cardboard and taped next to the screen, the four points from Elif's card. He had copied them when Elena had once shown them to him in the tram. “Also valid for control”, he wrote. Elif showed Elena the photo. Elena looked at it for a long time. Then she said: “No tram has run through Sibiu for a long time. My father still saw it as a child.” She smiled. “I think I'll have to build Dan one. Out of beeswax.”

That evening Elena went to the care home alone, without Elif, without an appointment, with a little jar of acacia honey. Mrs Petersen let her in, even though visiting hours were over. Grete lay in bed, very small, with her eyes closed, but when Elena sat down, she opened them. Elena told her about the test. About violins and melody. About Hotte, who was against everything, and Ludwig, who said “basically”. Grete listened, and her lips moved as if she were quietly speaking along with her. When Elena had finished, Grete said something, very quietly, so quietly that Elena had to lean forward. She didn't understand all the words. But she understood the melody. And the melody was: thank you. And: I'm tired. And: it's all right like this. Elena stayed there until Grete fell asleep and held her hand, which was as light as a sheet of paper.

On the way home, in the almost empty tram, Elena sat by the window and listened. She heard the hum of the overhead line, the squeal of the wheels on the curve at Eberswalder Straße, the voice of the announcement, which by now she knew by heart, and two young people right at the back, talking quietly in Italian and laughing. She didn't understand a word of Italian. But she understood that the two were in love, from the way they laughed. And she thought that in these five weeks in Berlin she had learned something that wasn't in any model test: that you can understand people without speaking their language, if you listen long enough. And that sometimes, as with Grete this evening, you can speak the language and still understand only the melody. And that the melody is enough. At the stop she got off, and the tram went on, ringing softly, into the dark, noisy, talkative city.
